text:
# Education in the Netherlands
The Dutch education system is coordinated by the Ministry of Education, Culture and Science, with compulsory education starting at age five and partial compulsory education continuing until 18 or diploma attainment. Schools can be public, special (often religious), or private, with public and special schools equally funded by the government. Children attend elementary school from ages 4 to 12, where they are assessed and guided towards appropriate secondary education based on standardized tests like the Cito Eindtoets. Secondary education splits into VMBO (vocational, 4 years), HAVO (general, 5 years), and VWO (academic, 6 years) tracks, with options for movement between levels. Higher education offers vocational HBO (universities of applied sciences) and academic WO (research universities) tracks with bachelor’s, master’s, and doctoral degrees. Education is widely inclusive, with special provisions for gifted and disabled students, though critiques note early tracking may limit late bloomers’ potential. International schools are present, and government inspection ensures quality across school types.

# Education in Japan
Japan’s education has roots in 6th-century Chinese influences, evolving through Buddhist and samurai schools to a modern system established in the Meiji Restoration, modeled after Western structures. Education is compulsory for nine years, covering six years of elementary and three years of lower secondary schooling. Upper secondary education is not compulsory but highly attended, with academic and vocational tracks available. Higher education includes universities, junior colleges, and specialized training institutions, offering bachelor’s, master’s, and doctoral degrees. The system emphasizes standardized curricula and exams, supplemented by significant "shadow education" (cram schools) due to intense exam competition. While achieving high literacy and academic performance, Japan faces criticism for academic pressure leading to student stress and insufficient development of creative and independent thinking. Recent reforms have focused on inclusive education for disabled students and reducing academic burdens.

text:
# Education in South Korea
South Korea’s education, deeply influenced by Confucian values, has evolved from traditional village and private academies to a highly centralized system emphasizing examination and meritocracy. The system comprises six years of elementary, three of middle, and three of high school education, with high school divided into general and vocational tracks, including special-purpose high schools (science, language, arts) and Meister vocational schools to revitalize technical education. Higher education is widespread and competitive, with strong emphasis on university degrees, especially from prestigious institutions ("SKY"). English education is a significant focus, supported by private tutoring ("hagwons"), though public English proficiency lags. Challenges include social stigma against vocational tracks, excessive academic pressure, mismatch between majors and jobs, and student health concerns due to the demanding education culture.

text:
# Education in Mexico
Mexico’s basic education consists of six years of primary, three years of junior high (secundaria), and three of high school (preparatoria or bachillerato), combining general and vocational tracks. Education reform mandated inclusion of special needs students, though challenges with integration, resource allocation, and teacher training persist. Although primary school attendance is high, secondary completion rates are moderate, and only a quarter pursue higher education. The higher education system aligns with the Bologna Process offering bachelor’s, master’s, and doctoral degrees, with intercultural universities addressing indigenous education gaps. Historically, education evolved from indigenous and colonial religious schools to a secular, nationally centralized system, with ongoing political and social challenges involving teacher unions and curriculum reforms. Mexico hosts over 150 international schools providing alternative curricula.

text:
# Education in Russia
Russia’s educational framework divides into general and professional education, with compulsory general education spanning preschool through secondary levels, culminating in an 11-year school program. Vocational education follows, with diverse specialized tracks. Higher education includes bachelor’s, specialist, master’s, and postgraduate degrees, evolving from a traditional single-stage specialist diploma to a Bologna-compatible two-tier system. Admission uses a unified state exam to standardize university entry. Special education caters to physical and mental disabilities with separate institutions and integration attempts. Russia has a vast tertiary education sector with numerous institutions, including elite universities mainly in Moscow and Saint Petersburg. Recent trends include controversial outreach laws and increased patriotic education aligned with government narratives. Language education reflects the country’s diversity, with numerous schools teaching minority languages.

text:
# Education in New Zealand
New Zealand offers free, compulsory primary and secondary education from age 6 to 16 (with many starting earlier), structured into 13 years (Year 1 to 13). Early childhood education is widely available with various centre-based and home-based options. The national curriculum guides teaching in eight learning areas, with qualifications such as the National Certificate of Educational Achievement (NCEA) at senior levels and alternatives like Cambridge and IB. School types include state, state-integrated (keeping religious or special character), and private schools. Māori language education has been revitalized alongside English-medium schooling. Funding is primarily government-supplied, supplemented by voluntary donations or attendance dues. Concerns include academic standards, particularly in mathematics, and school bullying. Extensive homeschooling and alternative schooling options exist but are minor in proportion.

# Education in Pakistan
Pakistan’s education system mirrors the British model, starting with pre-school and progressing through primary (years 1–5), middle (6–8), secondary (9–10), and higher secondary (11–12) education, followed by tertiary studies. The system includes general academic and technical/vocational streams, along with madrassas (religious schools) popular among poorer populations. Gender disparities persist, with lower female enrollment and literacy, although improvements are noted. Quality issues include outdated curricula, teacher shortages, and poor infrastructure. Tertiary education offers bachelor’s to doctoral degrees, but higher education access remains limited. Recent reforms focus on inclusion, technical education, and digital learning. Distance education and private international schools supplement formal education. Literacy rates have improved but remain below regional peers. The system faces criticism over religious influence and curriculum bias.

# Education in Saudi Arabia
Saudi Arabia’s education, initially rooted in Islamic and Quranic teaching, expanded with modern reforms since 1926, including free education at all levels managed primarily by the Ministry of Education. The system comprises kindergarten, six years of primary, three years of intermediate, and three years of secondary education with general and technical tracks. Girls’ education advanced amid cultural resistance, now constituting a majority in universities. Higher education offers bachelor’s to doctoral degrees across multiple universities, with extensive government scholarship programs for study abroad. Gifted education and special education have seen gradual development. Private and international schools operate under government oversight. The system is noted for heavy religious content and rote learning but is undergoing reforms for innovation and inclusivity. Criticism includes promotion of intolerance in curricula and insufficient preparation for a modern economy.

text:
# Education in Poland
Poland provides compulsory education starting at age six or seven, with recent reforms replacing a three-year junior high (gimnazjum) with eight years of primary school and adjusted secondary education. Secondary education offers general (liceum), technical (technikum), and vocational schools with final maturita exams granting university access. Tertiary education follows the Bologna system with bachelor’s, master’s, and doctoral programs, alongside vocational post-secondary schools. The grading system at university is numeric from 2 (fail) to 5 (excellent). Foreign language learning is emphasized, primarily English and German. Poland has a long educational history, with influences from European traditions and historic reforms shaping modern structure. Recent changes have sparked debate over curriculum focus and nationalism. Anti-violence policies have been intensified in response to school incidents.

text:
# Education in Bangladesh
Bangladesh’s education system includes pre-primary, primary, secondary, and tertiary levels with instruction in Bengali or English. The National Curriculum and Textbook Board standardizes education. Secondary students choose among science, commerce, or arts streams. The system faces challenges including resource constraints, high dropout rates in rural areas, and quality concerns such as rote learning. Religious education is incorporated with Islamic, Hindu, Buddhist, and Christian content, though non-Muslim students sometimes lack dedicated teachers. Technical and vocational education is available alongside mainstream education. International schools follow global curricula like IGCSE and IB. Efforts continue to improve female enrollment and literacy, which stood at roughly 75% in 2022. NGOs provide non-formal education, including refugee education for Rohingya children.

text:
# Education in the Czech Republic
The Czech education system begins with a nine-grade elementary school split into two stages, followed by various secondary education forms including vocational, professional, lyceum, grammar schools, and academies. Secondary education culminates in a standardized maturita exam necessary for university entrance. Special and practical schools serve students with developmental disabilities, with increasing inclusion efforts. Higher education consists of universities and higher professional schools offering bachelor’s, master’s, and doctoral degrees, along with specialized traditional academic titles. The school year runs from September to June, with multiple holidays and cultural observances. Private universities exist but public ones are predominant and generally regarded as higher-quality.

text:
# Education in Canada
In Canada, education is provincially managed, with compulsory schooling generally spanning kindergarten through grade 12, though variations exist by province. Early childhood education programs are widespread, with some provinces offering two-year kindergarten. The system includes public, state-integrated, private, and religious schools with diverse funding models. Postsecondary education is split between universities offering academic degrees and vocational institutions providing applied training, certificates, and diplomas. University admissions rely heavily on high school performance, with competitive programs imposing strict GPA cut-offs. Canada maintains constitutional protections for certain religious and language-based school systems, such as French-language schools and Catholic separate schools in provinces like Ontario. The quality of Canadian education is internationally recognized, though regional disparities and debates over equity data collection exist. The federal government’s educational role is limited, primarily focusing on Indigenous education and military academies.
